```python
import sqlite3


def save_filter(db, label, name):
    db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO saved_filters (label, name) VALUES (?, ?) "
        "ON CONFLICT(label) DO UPDATE SET name = excluded.name",
        (label, name),
    )
    return None


def search_saved_filter(db, label):
    cursor = db.execute(
        "SELECT p.id, p.name "
        "FROM products AS p "
        "JOIN saved_filters AS f ON p.name = f.name "
        "WHERE f.label = ? "
        "ORDER BY p.id ASC",
        (label,),
    )
    return [(row[0], row[1]) for row in cursor.fetchall()]
```

Both functions use parameterized queries, so untrusted `label` and `name` values can't inject SQL. The upsert replaces the stored name when the label already exists. `search_saved_filter` uses `=` for an exact, case-sensitive match on the name (SQLite's default BINARY collation, unlike `LIKE`, which treats `%` and `_` as wildcards). It returns an empty list when the label is missing or nothing matches. The functions never commit, roll back, or close the connection.

The upsert syntax (`ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`) requires SQLite 3.24 or newer. On older versions, `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO saved_filters (label, name) VALUES (?, ?)` is an equivalent alternative here, since the table has only two columns.
